job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half six and I'm at my desk in a Birmingham insurer's data team by nine. I'm a junior data engineer, so I build and mend the pipelines that move claims data from one system to another. Half my day is an AI coding assistant open next to my editor, and the other half is my team lead, Joanne, telling me why my first answer was wrong. Evenings I work on a little app for my parents' friends who run market stalls, and then I play five-a-side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and how did the job come about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science at Aston, a 2:1, with one summer internship at a bus company building dashboards. The insurer hired me through a graduate scheme in the spring, and I started in July. I share a flat in Digbeth with my cousin Kwabena, and my parents run a small import shop in Handsworth. I have about two months of costs saved and around ten thousand in loan, so I'm not rich, but my parents would help me if I got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I'd bet on, to be honest, and I'd be a bit disappointed. I use these tools every day, and they're good but they make plenty of mistakes. At work I'd say they save me an hour or two a day and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. Nothing big changes, so I get to be a data engineer for ten years and move up slowly. My own worry is that my pay stays typical entry pay, the rent keeps going up, and I'm still paying a loan in my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day job and push on with the stall-holders' app, because it's a real chance to earn some extra. I'd try to charge three or four of my parents' friends about fifteen pounds a month each. And I'd keep going with the courses on cloud systems, since promotions go to people who can run the whole pipeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. A bit bored, even, if I'm honest. I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really think the stall app could make money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, maybe a hundred pounds a month if it goes well. But it teaches me to sell and support something real, and nobody at the insurer teaches that. It also means I have a second thing if the job goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine, but you also mentioned rent and the loan. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'm fine about work and I'm stretched about money. A graduate pay cheque in Birmingham covers a shared flat and food, and not much more. The loan hangs over me in a quiet way, and I'd be lying if I said it didn't.

They save me an hour or two a day, **no more**.
think: I'd be a data engineer for **ten years**, moving up slowly.
My worry is **entry pay**, rising rent and a loan into my thirties.
do: Push on with the **stall-holders' app** and charge a few of my parents' friends.
Keep taking **cloud systems** courses so I can run a whole pipeline.
feel: **Relaxed**, a little bored, because I like change.
S0.quote: The loan hangs over me in a quiet way, and I'd be lying if I said it didn't.
fieldNote: Calm about the **job**, honest about the money; he says both.
The side app is as much about learning to **sell** as about income.
Daily AI user, so he judges the tools by their mistakes.

steps.text: Sign three market traders to the stall app at 15 pounds a month
Finish the cloud data pipelines course by spring
Keep building claims data pipelines at the insurer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, but let's be straight about who gets hurt. At work I'd say we should use the tools more, not less. Online I'd say there should be training for people whose jobs shrink, and the firms making money from it should help pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot, but not a safe one. I already use AI daily, so I'm ahead of most of my team. But a lot of what a junior does, like writing basic code and checking data, is exactly what the tools can take. The firm might need fewer juniors and a few more senior people who check the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person on the team who knows the AI tools best, and I'd offer to run a session for the others. I'd turn the stall app into something I can show, like a small portfolio, and put it on GitHub. And I'd start learning how to design systems, not just write code, because design is harder for AI to take away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of nerves. It feels like being at the front of a wave rather than under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joanne's older colleague, Mick, who's been writing these pipelines for twenty years. He doesn't use AI at all and he's brilliant at the edge cases. I'd want to sit with him and show him how I use it. I'd feel bad if the firm cut my older colleague Mick and kept me because I'm cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'learning to design systems' mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means asking why a pipeline is built a certain way, not just making it run. I'd ask Joanne to let me sit in her design meetings once a week. I'd also read two or three books on architecture. By next summer I'd like to design one small system myself.

Firms making money from it should help pay for **training**.

Learn **system design** by sitting in Joanne's design meetings.

Plan to move from writing code to **designing** systems.

steps.text: Run an hour-long AI tools session for the data team
Put the stall app on GitHub with a short write-up
Sit in Joanne's weekly design meeting and read two architecture books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and anyone who says they are is selling something. At work I'd ask for a plan, though I doubt we'd get one. Online I'd say the first thing needed is public support, like a basic income, because a lot of jobs go at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. I code with AI every day, so I can see how fast it gets better, and I know full AI can do my whole job. The insurer would only need a few people to oversee it. My degree is worth much less, and I only get a head start of about three years before robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard, pay every spare pound into savings and stop buying new trainers and games. I'd ask my parents if I could be a partner in the shop for a while, because the shop is hands-on and sells to people who like a human face. I'd also keep working on the app, because anything I can sell directly to real customers is worth more than a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared but sort of alert. I think I'd throw myself into doing things, because sitting still would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think a shop is safer than the insurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028, anyway. Thinking work goes first, so insurers and software firms get hit before a corner shop does. Robots reach hands-on work around 2031, and even then my parents' customers like talking to a person. It's not a forever plan, but it's a shelter while things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad that the job might go in a year or two, and that I'd like to help in the shop. My dad would say, I didn't send you to university to carry boxes. And my mum would say, he's allowed to. That would be a long evening.

The first thing needed is **public support**, like a basic income.

fieldNote: Knows the **tools** best of all nine, and that makes him more frightened.

steps.text: Stop buying new trainers and games for a year
Move every spare pound into a savings account
Offer to work in my parents' import shop on weekends
Sign up more stall holders for the app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a lot of time to do something good with. At work I'd push our team to plan and retrain people now. Online I'd back training funds, and I'd say the firms that profit should pay a fair share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is what I've been preparing for. I'd have five years to change my skills, and I'm someone who likes to try things. I'd still worry about the competition, though, because plenty of other graduates would try to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to get promoted to mid-level in about three years, and I'd keep the app going and try to make it into an actual small firm. I'd also study part-time for a master's, maybe in AI systems, if the insurer pays. And I'd put a third of my pay into savings, so I'd have at least a year of costs by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty positive, a little nervous. It feels like a race I can enter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind and make you more worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw graduates at other firms being let go in big numbers. That would be a signal. I'd start counting how many junior jobs are on the board every month, because the numbers tell you more than the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kwabena, your cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's an accountant, so he's in the same boat. I'd tell Kwabena to start learning the tools now and to keep one hands-on skill, like looking after his dad's rental flats. We'd probably keep each other honest over a curry on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different thing. I'd say it's a gift and we should use it for retraining and sensible rules. At work I'd say the firm should plan a career ladder that still works when AI does the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. I'd be 32, and I'd have time to build real skills, maybe my own firm. The danger is that ten years makes everyone complacent, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my day job a few years, then probably jump to a small firm or start one with my cousin Kwabena, where I'd learn more. I'd keep investing in the app and in the stall holders' network. I'd put money into a small index fund every month, because I'd have the time to let it grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Properly good. I'd feel like I had room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you invest in, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A global index fund, about a hundred pounds a month. Nothing clever. If AI makes companies much richer, I'd want a small piece of that, since my wages might not rise with it. It's a hedge more than a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to feeling this good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I could waste a few years. I'd set myself a rule: every year in November I write down what I've learned and what I've shipped. If the list is empty I'd know I've drifted.

The firm should plan a **career ladder** that still works.

Ten years can make everyone **complacent**, including me.

S4.quote: If AI makes companies much richer, I'd want a small piece of that, since my wages might not rise with it.
fieldNote: Takes the **investing** logic of a hedge: own a slice of what replaces wages.

Fully at ease with change, as his profile says.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build anything. What would help is public support that kicks in quickly, retraining that doesn't cost me more debt, and an employer who tells the truth early. I'd also like the tools to stay cheap and open for people who can't pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume young people who use AI every day are relaxed about it. I'm not. I'm excited and frightened at the same time, and I think more people my age are than say so.

headlineQuote: I'm excited and frightened at the same time, and I think more people my age are than say so.
portrait: Hassan Mensah is **22**, a junior data engineer at a Birmingham insurer, sharing a flat in Digbeth with his cousin.
He did computer science at Aston, owes about **ten thousand** and has two months of costs saved.
He's progressive and adaptive, uses **AI every day**, and runs a small app for his parents' friends who have market stalls.
He's calm in mild worlds, **anxious** at AGI in two years, and in that world retreats to his parents' shop.
With more time he plans a master's, an **index fund** and maybe a firm with his cousin.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be **no time** to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **public support**, retraining without more debt, and an employer who tells the truth early.
